# Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/early-morning-waking/

Why does my baby wake at 5 a.m., and how do I fix it?
Early waking is almost always a schedule problem, a light problem, or a sleep-association problem — usually in that order. Check that bedtime is not too late (overtiredness causes early waking, counterintuitively), that the room is fully dark at 5 a.m., and that your baby can fall back asleep without your help. Then hold a firm “morning starts at 6” line for two weeks.
Work through the causes in order
Bedtime too late. An overtired baby produces more cortisol and sleeps lighter in the early morning. Try moving bedtime 30 minutes earlier for a week. This fixes more early waking than anything else.
Naps too long or too late. A late afternoon nap or too much total daytime sleep lowers sleep pressure for the end of the night. Cap the last nap so it ends by about 4 p.m.
Light. The sun is up, or a hallway light is on. Early morning sleep is the lightest of the night; any light becomes a cue to wake. Blackout the room properly — test it at 5 a.m.
Sleep association. The 5 a.m. waking is a cycle transition, and the baby cannot get back down without the bedtime method. Solving bedtime solves 5 a.m.
Reinforced waking. If 5 a.m. means milk, a parent’s bed or screen time, it becomes the best part of the day. Keep the morning boring until the set wake time.
Hunger is occasionally real in a baby under 6 months or one dropping a night feed. Offer more during the day.
The hold-the-line protocol
Choose a wake time (6 a.m. is realistic for most babies). Before that time, treat the waking exactly as you would a 2 a.m. waking: same response, no milk, no lights, no leaving the room for the day. At the set time, open the curtains, turn on lights, greet cheerfully. The contrast teaches the clock. Expect 1–2 weeks.
Frequently asked
Is 6 a.m. a normal wake time for a baby?Yes. Most babies wake between 6 and 7 a.m. Getting a baby to sleep until 8 is rarely realistic.
Will a later bedtime make my baby sleep later?Usually the opposite. Overtiredness causes earlier waking. Try earlier first.
Do toddler sleep-training clocks work?They help from about 2.5–3 years, once the child understands the color change. They do not work for babies.

# Why does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/short-naps-30-minutes/

Why does my baby only nap for 30 minutes, and how do I lengthen naps?
A 30–45 minute nap is one sleep cycle; the baby wakes at the transition and cannot link to the next cycle. The usual causes are a wake window that is slightly off, a sleep association that worked at nap onset but is missing at the transition, or a room that is not dark enough. Fix the schedule first, teach independent sleep onset at bedtime, then give the nap a chance to extend by waiting a few minutes before intervening.
Why naps are the last thing to improve
Daytime sleep pressure is lower, naps are short by nature in the first months, and the body’s clock does not help as it does at night. Many babies under 5–6 months take short naps regardless of anything you do; it is developmental. Past that age, short naps are fixable.
The checklist
Schedule. Both too short and too long a wake window produce a 30-minute nap. Adjust by 15 minutes, hold for three days.
Onset. If the baby falls asleep being fed or rocked, the cycle transition reproduces the problem. Nap onset should look like bedtime onset: down awake.
Environment. Darker than you think. White noise continuous, not on a timer. Comfortable temperature.
The pause. When the baby stirs at 30 minutes, wait a set number of minutes before going in. Many babies resettle if given the chance; going in immediately ends the nap every time.
Crib hour. For babies over 5–6 months, keep the nap period to a consistent length in the crib even if the sleep is short, so the body learns the window. Do not leave a distressed baby; this is for a calm or grumbling baby.
Rescue the day. After a short nap, shorten the next wake window a little so overtiredness does not compound.
Realistic expectations
Nights usually improve in a week. Naps typically take 2–4 weeks after that to consolidate, and the first nap of the day lengthens first. Short afternoon catnaps are normal until the 3-to-2 transition.
Frequently asked
Are 30 minute naps normal?Under about 5 months, yes. Past 6 months, consistent 30-minute naps usually mean a schedule or sleep-association issue.
Should I wake my baby from a long nap?Cap naps that would push bedtime late, and wake a newborn for feeds if your pediatrician says so. Otherwise a long nap is fine.
Can I hold my baby for one nap a day?If you want to, yes — choose which one and keep it consistent so the baby knows what to expect at the others.

# My toddler won’t stay in bed. How do I fix it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/toddler-wont-stay-in-bed/

My toddler won’t stay in bed. How do I fix it?
First, if your child is under 3 and still fits safely in a crib, consider going back to it; most bed problems are a too-early crib exit. If a bed is where you are, the fix is a short consistent routine, a clear rule (“we stay in bed until the light turns green”), and a boring, silent, repeated return to bed every single time they get up — dozens of times the first night if needed, fewer each night after. Most toddlers stop within one to two weeks.
Before anything else: crib or bed?
The AAP suggests waiting until closer to 3 for a bed unless the child is climbing out dangerously. A 20-month-old in a bed has freedom with no impulse control. If you moved early, moving back is not a failure; it is often the fastest fix. If climbing is the issue, lower the mattress, use a sleep sack (it limits leg lift), and remove anything used as a step.
If the bed is staying
Make the room safe enough to be unsupervised. Anchored furniture, covered outlets, a gate or closed door, nothing climbable. Assume the child will be up alone.
A short routine with a clear ending. Same order nightly, 20–30 minutes, ending with one phrase that means “done.” No renegotiation after it.
State the rule once. “You stay in bed until the light is green.” A toddler clock helps from about 2.5 years.
The silent return. Every time the child gets up, walk them back without talking, without eye contact, without a cuddle, and leave. The first night may be 30–50 returns. It drops fast when the payoff is zero.
Pre-empt the requests. Water bottle in reach, last bathroom trip in the routine, one “bedtime pass” they can trade for one visit if that fits your child.
Morning reward, not bedtime bribes: a sticker or praise at wake-up for staying in bed.
What makes it worse
Lying down with them “just tonight.” Letting them fall asleep on the couch. Long explanations at 9 p.m. Getting angry (attention is attention). Inconsistency between parents. Each of these resets the count.
Frequently asked
Should I lock my toddler’s door?A gate at the door or a door knob cover is a common compromise; many families use a closed door for safety. Whatever you choose, the room itself must be fully childproofed.
How long will the silent return take to work?Typically a dramatic drop in 3–4 nights and near-zero in 1–2 weeks, if it is done every time.
My toddler is scared of the dark. Is that real?Fears emerge around 2–3 years and are real. A dim warm nightlight and a consistent, calm response help; staying in the room until they fall asleep tends to prolong it.

# Why is my 8, 9 or 10 month old suddenly waking at night?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/8-to-10-month-sleep-regression/

Why is my 8, 9 or 10 month old suddenly waking at night?
The 8–10 month period stacks three things at once: new gross motor skills (crawling, pulling to stand) that get practiced in the crib, the peak of separation anxiety, and the 3-to-2 nap transition. Keep the response to night waking exactly what it was, practice the new skills in daylight, protect two solid naps, and expect 2–3 weeks. A previously independent sleeper usually returns to baseline in a few nights.
What is happening
Motor leaps. A baby who just learned to stand will stand up in the crib at 2 a.m. and may not know how to get down. Practice sitting down from standing during the day, many times. At night, lay them down once and leave; repeating it becomes a game.
Separation anxiety. Object permanence has arrived: the baby now knows you exist when you leave, and protests. A predictable routine and a brief, confident goodbye reassure more than lingering does.
Nap transition. The third nap is disappearing, and a day with too little daytime sleep produces a worse night. Move bedtime earlier on short-nap days.
Teething and illness ride along but rarely explain weeks of waking.
What to do
Do not introduce anything new at night: no return of night feeds, rocking to sleep or bed-sharing unless you plan to keep them.
Hold the nap schedule; two naps totaling 2.5–3.5 hours; bedtime 6:30–7:30 p.m.
Daytime practice for every new skill, especially getting down from standing.
If the baby never slept independently, this is a fine age to start; separation anxiety is not a reason to wait, and the plan accounts for it.
Frequently asked
How long does the 8 month sleep regression last?Typically 2–3 weeks with a consistent response; longer if new habits are introduced during it.
Should I feed my 9 month old at night during the regression?If your baby was not feeding at night before, do not restart. Offer more during the day.
My baby stands in the crib and cries. What do I do?Lay them down once, calmly, and leave. Then practice sitting down from standing during the day until they can do it alone.

# Is the 18 month sleep regression real, and what do I do about it?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/18-month-sleep-regression/

Is the 18 month sleep regression real, and what do I do about it?
Yes, and it is mostly a toddler-development story: new independence and testing, language exploding faster than self-control, separation anxiety returning, molars, and the 2-to-1 nap transition. The fix is boundaries, not new comforts: a tight routine, the same response every night, two naps held until they are clearly done, and patience for 2–6 weeks.
Why 18 months is different
Earlier regressions are about sleep physiology. This one is about a person: an 18-month-old wants control, has opinions, and has discovered that bedtime protest gets a reaction. It overlaps with molars (real but brief), the nap transition (real and long), and a second wave of separation anxiety.
What works
Routine with limited choices. “Red pajamas or blue?” gives control where it is harmless. The order and the ending do not change.
Same response at night. Brief, boring, consistent. Toddlers are expert at finding the one thing that works on you.
Nap schedule. If still on two naps, hold them until the second is refused for two weeks. If transitioning, one nap around midday and an early bedtime.
Keep the crib. This is not the moment to move to a bed. Regressions and transitions compound.
Daytime connection. Twenty minutes of undivided attention before the routine reduces bedtime stalling more than most tricks.
Molars and medicine
First molars often arrive around 13–19 months and can hurt. Pain relief for a clearly uncomfortable toddler, as your pediatrician directs, is reasonable for a night or two. A new sleep habit started during those nights will outlast the tooth by months.
Frequently asked
How long does the 18 month regression last?Two to six weeks is typical. It runs longer when new habits are introduced during it.
Should I move my 18 month old to a toddler bed?No. Most experts suggest waiting until closer to 3 unless there is a safety reason.
Is my toddler manipulating me?Testing, not manipulating. Toddlers learn what works. A calm, consistent response teaches them that protest does not change the outcome.

# How do you sleep train twins?
URL: https://actuallysleepingllc.com/guides/sleep-training-twins/

How do you sleep train twins?
The same way as one baby, on the same schedule, in the same room, with the expectation that one will wake the other less often than you fear. Synchronize feeds and naps from the start, put both down awake at the same time, respond to each by the plan rather than rushing to prevent noise, and accept that the first week is louder. Most twin families see both babies sleeping through within the same two weeks.
Principles that matter more with twins
Same schedule, always. If one wakes to feed, feed both (or wake the other within 15–20 minutes). Staggered twins mean no sleep for anyone.
Same room. Twins habituate to each other’s noise faster than you expect. Separating them for training usually just postpones the problem. White noise helps.
Do not referee. Rushing in to keep one from waking the other teaches both that crying brings you fast. Follow the plan for each baby individually.
Treat them as individuals within the plan. One may be a faster learner; the plan accounts for temperament. Do not hold the easier sleeper to the harder one’s pace.
Two adults, one method. Decide in advance who handles which baby and that both respond identically.
Premature twins
Many twins arrive early. Use corrected age for readiness, get the pediatrician’s sign-off on night feeds for each baby separately, and expect that weight gain, not the calendar, decides when night feeds go.
Why coaching helps disproportionately for twins
There is twice as much data every night and half as much parental capacity to interpret it. A coach reading both babies’ logs each morning and telling you which adjustment to make is the difference between a hard week and a hard season.
Frequently asked
Will one twin wake the other?Occasionally in the first days, then rarely. Babies habituate to a roommate quickly; adults are usually the ones who cannot sleep through it.
Should twins sleep in the same crib?No. The AAP recommends a separate sleep surface for each baby.
Can twins be on different schedules?They can, but it doubles the work and is rarely sustainable. Synchronize feeds and naps as early as possible.
ReferencesAmerican Academy of Pediatrics. Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment. Pediatrics. 2022.
